{\mathrm{wt}}(E|_{W})+{\mathrm{wt}}(E|_{V\setminus W})={\mathrm{wt}}(E)\leq{\mathrm{wt}}(F)={\mathrm{wt}}(F|_{W})+{\mathrm{wt}}(F|_{V\setminus W})\,.

(465)

If
{\mathrm{wt}}(E|_{W})>{\mathrm{wt}}(F|_{W})
then we can choose
E^{\prime}
such that
E^{\prime}|_{W}=F|_{W}
and
E^{\prime}|_{V\setminus W}=E|_{V\setminus W}
so that
s(E^{\prime})=s(F|_{W})+s(E|_{V\setminus W})=s(F|_{W})+s(F|_{V\setminus W})=s(F)
and
{\mathrm{wt}}(E^{\prime})<{\mathrm{wt}}(E)
(
s(E|_{V\setminus W})=s(F|_{V\setminus W})
follows from property 2 above that
s(EF|_{V\setminus W})=0
).
This contradicts that
E
is a minimum weight error with syndrome equal to
s(F)
, therefore
{\mathrm{wt}}(E|_{W})\leq{\mathrm{wt}}(F|_{W})
must be true.
So,

|W|={\mathrm{wt}}(EF|_{W})\leq{\mathrm{wt}}(E|_{W})+{\mathrm{wt}}(F|_{W})\leq 2{\mathrm{wt}}(F|_{W})

(466)

which implies that
{\mathrm{wt}}(F|_{W})\geq|W|/2
, completing the proof

We have shown that a decoding failure implies that there exists a set of connected qubits
W\subseteq V(G)
of size
|W|\geq d_{i}
such that at least
|W|/2
of the qubits in it are faulty.
Thus, the probability of a logical error resulting from decoding failure for a Pauli error
F
and (incorrect) correction Pauli
E
can be bounded as

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{Logical error}]

\displaystyle=\Pr[EF\in\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{S}_{i})\setminus\mathcal{S}_{i}]

(467)

\displaystyle\leq\Pr{\exists W\subseteq V(G) : W\text{ connected}\,,\; |W|\geq d_i \,,\; \wt(F|_W)\geq\lceil|W|/2\rceil}

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}W\subseteq V(G):\\
|W|\geq d_{i}\,,\\
W\text{ connected}\end{subarray}}\Pr[{\mathrm{wt}}(F|_{W})\geq\lceil|W|/2\rceil]\,,

by using a union bound to obtain the second inequality.
To obtain an upper bound for the logical error in terms of physical error rate
p
and the code parameters, we need to put a bound on the number of the connected sets in the sum of
Equation

467
and the probability of more than half erroneous qubits in a set.

For a qubit
v\in V(G)
, the number of subsets of connected qubits
W\subseteq V(G)
of size
|W|=q
containing
v
can be upper bounded using Lemma 2 of Ref.
[
113
]
as

|\{W\subseteq V(G):|W|=q\,,\;W\text{ connected}\,,\;v\in W\}|\leq\deg(v)e^{q-1}\,.

(468)

Since there are
n_{i}
qubits in total and the degree of each qubit is bounded by
(r-1)c
(c.f.
Equation

464
), therefore the total number of connected subsets of size
q
in
G
is bounded as

|\{W\subseteq V(G):|W|=q\,,\;\text{$W$ connected}\}|\leq n_{i}((r-1)ce)^{q-1}\,.

(469)

On the other hand, for a subset
W\subseteq V(G)
, the probability that there are
\lceil|W|/2\rceil
erroneous qubits in
W
is bounded by

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{$\lceil q/2\rceil$ errors in $W$}]

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{T\subseteq W:|T|=\lceil|W|/2\rceil}\Pr[\text{all qubits in $T$ are faulty}]

(470)

\displaystyle\leq\binom{q}{\lceil q/2\rceil}p^{\lceil q/2\rceil}\leq 2^{q}p^{\lceil q/2\rceil}

by the union bound and the local stochastic noise assumption (c.f.
).

Thus, we can further bound the inequality in
Equation

467
as

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{Logical error}]

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}W\subseteq V(G):\\
|W|\geq d_{i}\,,\\
W\text{ connected}\end{subarray}}\Pr[{\mathrm{wt}}(F|_{W})\geq\lceil|W|/2\rceil]

(471)

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{q=d_{i}}^{\infty}|\{W\subseteq V(G):|W|=q\,,\;W\text{ connected}\,,\;v\in W\}|

\displaystyle\times\Pr[\text{$\lceil q/2\rceil$ errors in $W$}]

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{q=1}^{\infty}n_{i}((r-1)ce)^{q-1}2^{q}p^{\lceil q/2\rceil}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{n_{i}}{(r-1)ce}\sum_{q=1}^{\infty}(2(r-1)ce\sqrt{p})^{q}\,.

The series
\sum_{q=1}^{\infty}(2(r-1)ce\sqrt{p})^{q}
is a geometric series and therefore converges to
\frac{(2(r-1)ce\sqrt{p})^{d_{i}}}{1-(2(r-1)ce\sqrt{p})}
whenever
2(r-1)ce\sqrt{p}<1
.
So we can define the threshold as
p_{0}=(2(r-1)ce)^{-2}
so that whenever
p<p_{0}
we have
(2(r-1)ce\sqrt{p}<1
and by denoting
\alpha=(r-1)ce
we have

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{Logical error}]

\displaystyle\leq\frac{n_{i}}{\alpha}\frac{(2\alpha\sqrt{p})^{d_{i}}}{1-(2\alpha\sqrt{p})}\leq\frac{n_{i}}{\alpha(1-(2\alpha\sqrt{p}))}\Big(\frac{p}{p_{0}}\Big)^{d_{i}/2}\,,

(472)

since
2\alpha\sqrt{p}=\sqrt{p/p_{0}}
.
So, the logical error probability
p_{L}
is bounded as
p_{L}\leq O(n_{i}(p/p_{0})^{d_{i}/2})
as claimed (the
\sqrt{p}
in the denominator is absorbed into the
O
and
\alpha=(r-1)ce
is a constant independent of the code parameter).

14.3
Decoding threshold for noisy syndrome extraction

In the last section, we showed that a family of qLDPC codes
\llbracket n_{i},k_{i},d_{i}\rrbracket
with growing physical qubits and distance (
n_{i}\rightarrow\infty
and
d_{i}\rightarrow\infty
as
i\rightarrow\infty
) can be decoded with exponential logical error suppression whenever the physical error rate is below a certain threshold, under local stochastic noise model.
However, this assumes that the syndrome extraction process itself is noiseless, that is, the syndrome extraction (SE) circuit implementing stabilizer measurements is ideal.
In a realistic scenario, components inside the SE circuit can themselves be faulty.
To model a realistic scenario more faithfully, besides qubit errors on the input state, we also need to consider a circuit-level noise model in the QEC procedure, which consists of both qubit errors and measurement errors in the SE circuit.

Theorem 4 of
[
113
]
shows that even if SE circuits are noisy, a qLDPC code family whose parameters satisfy the aforementioned properties can also be decoded with exponential logical error suppression given that initial error rate per qubit
\tilde{p}
, error rate per qubit at each SE cycle
p
, and bit-flip error rate per syndrome bit
q
are below certain thresholds, under the circuit-level local stochastic noise model.
Such error suppression is obtained when we repeat the SE circuit
T=d_{i}
many times where syndromes between subsequent SE cycles are compared to infer syndromes reliably.
In this section, we discuss the proof of this result in detail.

14.3.1
Errors in the syndrome extraction circuit

As mentioned above, we first need to consider input errors, syndrome bit errors (resulting from faulty measurements), and gate errors.
For this, we consider the following errors at each step
t\in[1,T]
in the SE cycle:

1.

F_{t}\in\mathcal{P}_{n}
the actual
n
-qubit physical Pauli errors at timestep
t
and
E_{t}\in\mathcal{P}_{n}
physical Pauli errors deduced by the decoder (i.e., which physical errors the decoder thinks happened at round
t
).

2.

B_{t}\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}^{l}
the set of actual syndrome bit errors at timestep
t
and
C_{t}\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}^{l}
are the sets of syndrome bit errors deduced by the decoder (i.e., which bit-flip errors the decoder thinks happened in round
t
).

3.

F_{1}
and
E_{1}
are actual and deduced input errors, respectively.

Physical errors in
F_{t}
are those that can trigger a detection in round
t
SE.
We can express physical error
F_{t}
and syndrome bit error
B_{t}
as
F_{t}=F_{t,1}\otimes\dots\otimes F_{t,n}
and
B_{t}=(B_{t,1},\dots,B_{t,l})
where
F_{t,q}
are Pauli errors on qubit
q
at timestep
t
and
B_{t,j}
are bit-flip errors on syndrome measurement for stabilizer generator
g_{j}
at round
t
.
To illustrate this, consider the following example.

Example 14.2

(label=ex:repetition_SE_circuit)
.

A 3-round SE circuit for the 4-qubit bit-flip repetition code is given by

}\end{gathered}

(473)

A noisy implementation of this 3-round SE circuit is therefore given by

\begin{gathered}\resizebox{20348790}{}{

\gate[2,style={fill=blue!10}]{M_{ZZ}} \gategroup[4,steps=3,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=blue!05, inner xsep=2pt},background,label style={label position=above,anchor=north,yshift=0.4cm}]{{SE cycle 2 w/ error $F_{3}$}} \wire[d][5][""{above,pos=-0.3}]{c} {\\

\gate[2,style={fill=blue!10}]{M_{ZZ}} \wire[d][4][""{above,pos=-0.3}]{c} {\\
}
\gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{F_{1,3}} \gate[2,style={fill=blue!10}]{M_{ZZ}} \wire[d][3][""{above,pos=-0.3}]{c} \gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{F_{2,3}}
\gate[2,style={fill=blue!10}]{M_{ZZ}} \wire[d][3][""{above,pos=-0.3}]{c} \gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{F_{3,3}}
\gate[2,style={fill=blue!10}]{M_{ZZ}} \wire[d][3][""{above,pos=-0.3}]{c} {\\
}
\gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{F_{1,4}} \gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{F_{2,4}}
\gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{F_{3,4}}
{\\

\setwiretype{n} \gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{B_{1,1}} \gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{B_{1,2}} \gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{B_{1,3}}
\gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{B_{2,1}} \gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{B_{2,2}} \gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{B_{2,3}}
\gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{B_{3,1}} \gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{B_{3,2}} \gate[1,style={dashed,rounded corners,fill=red!10}]{B_{3,3}} {\\
}
\setwiretype{n} \gate[1,style={blue!0,fill=blue!0,fill opacity=0,opacity=0}]{s_{1,1}} \gate[1,style={blue!0,fill=blue!0,fill opacity=0,opacity=0}]{s_{1,2}} \gate[1,style={blue!0,fill=blue!0,fill opacity=0,opacity=0}]{s_{1,3}}
\gate[1,style={blue!0,fill=blue!0,fill opacity=0,opacity=0}]{s_{2,1}} \gate[1,style={blue!0,fill=blue!0,fill opacity=0,opacity=0}]{s_{2,2}} \gate[1,style={blue!0,fill=blue!0,fill opacity=0,opacity=0}]{s_{2,3}}
\gate[1,style={blue!0,fill=blue!0,fill opacity=0,opacity=0}]{s_{3,1}} \gate[1,style={blue!0,fill=blue!0,fill opacity=0,opacity=0}]{s_{3,2}} \gate[1,style={blue!0,fill=blue!0,fill opacity=0,opacity=0}]{s_{3,3}}
}\end{gathered}

(474)

Now, let
\sigma(F_{t})\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}^{l}
and
\sigma(E_{t})\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}^{l}
be the syndromes for Pauli errors
F_{t}
and
E_{t}
, respectively, before accounting for syndrome bit errors.

\sigma
maps Pauli errors to bit strings so that the syndrome of the product of two errors is the sum of their individual syndromes, that is,
\sigma(FF^{\prime})=\sigma(F)+\sigma(F^{\prime})
. In other words,
\sigma
is a homomorphism from Pauli errors to bit strings.
Note that the syndrome
s_{t}
that we observe from timestep
t
SE takes into account the cumulative errors
D_{t-1}=F_{t-1}\dots F_{1}
from timesteps
1
to
t-1
as well as timestep-
t
physical errors
F_{t}
and measurement errors
B_{t}
.
So the syndrome with perfect measurement from time-
t
SE is given by
\sigma(F_{t}D_{t-1})=\sigma(F_{t})+\sigma(D_{t-1})
and thus

s_{t}=\sigma(F_{t}D_{t-1})+B_{t}=\sigma(F_{t})+\sigma(D_{t-1})+B_{t}\,.

(475)

We call
s_{t}
the
observed
syndrome from SE at timestep
t
(note that
s_{t}
depends on
F_{1},\dots,F_{t}
and
B_{t}
, but not on
B_{1},\dots,B_{t-1}
since these are errors on syndrome measurements from timestep
1
to
t
, which do not affect the measurement outcomes at timestep
t
).
To further clarify this, consider the following example.

Example 14.3

(label=ex:syndromes)
.

Observed syndromes and cumulative errors
Consider a syndrome extraction for a 4-qubit repetition code illustrated in
stabilizer generators
g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}
.
Note that the cumulative errors at the end of timestep
1
is
D_{1}=F_{1}
, and suppose that it flips
g_{1}
and
g_{2}
so that
\sigma(F_{1})=(1,0,1)
where there is no measurement errors, that is,
B_{1}=(0,0,0)
.
Thus, the syndromes observed at
t=1
SE is

s_{1}=\sigma(F_{1})+B_{1}=\sigma(F_{1})=(1,0,1)\,.

(476)

If there are no errors between timesteps
1
and
2
, that is,
F_{2}=I
and
\sigma(F_{2})=(0,0,0)
, and for measurement errors
B_{2}=(0,0,1)
in the second round of SE, then the observed syndrome at
t=2
is

s_{2}=\sigma(F_{2}D_{1})+B_{2}=\sigma(F_{1})+B_{2}=(1,0,0)\,.

(477)

Namely, the observed syndrome
s_{2}
from
t=2
SE is the observed syndrome from SE at
t=1
with its third bit flipped due to measurement error
B_{2}=(0,0,1)
.

The observed syndrome from timestep-
t
SE cycle is given by
\sigma(F_{t})+B_{t}
, where syndrome bit errors
B_{t}
are taken into account.
Also, we define the change between observed syndromes at timestep
t-1
and
t
as

\displaystyle\Delta_{t}

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}s_{t-1}+s_{t}\quad&,\quad t\geq 2\\
s_{1}\quad&,\quad t=1\,.\end{cases}

(478)

Since
D_{t}=F_{t}D_{t-1}
therefore we can write the observed syndrome change
\Delta_{t}
as

\displaystyle\Delta_{t}

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\sigma(F_{t})+B_{t}+B_{t-1}\quad&,\quad t\geq 2\\
\sigma(F_{t})+B_{t}\quad&,\quad t=1\,,\end{cases}

(479)

where the syndrome at timestep
t=1
is compared to the all-zero syndrome, that is, the syndrome corresponding to an ideal initial codestate
|\overline{\psi}\rangle
.
Syndrome change
\Delta_{t}=\sigma(F_{t})+B_{t}+B_{t-1}
is basically the difference between observed syndromes between
t-1
and
t
SE rounds.

Example 14.4

(label=ex:syndrome_change)
.

Observed syndrome change
Continuing
, recall that the syndromes due to physical errors
F_{1}
and
F_{2}
are given by
\sigma(F_{1})=(1,0,1)
and
\sigma(F_{2})=(0,0,0)
, respectively.
Note that syndrome change
\Delta_{2}
takes into account
new
errors
F_{2}
between timesteps
1
and
2
, as well as measurement errors
B_{1}=(0,0,0)
and
B_{2}=(0,0,1)
.
So, it is given by

\Delta_{2}=s_{1}+s_{2}=(\sigma(F_{1})+B_{1})+(\sigma(F_{2}D_{1})+B_{2})=\sigma(F_{2})+B_{1}+B_{2}=(0,0,1)\,,

(480)

indicating that the syndrome
g_{3}
has been flipped (in this case due to measurement error
B_{2}
).

Now suppose that at
t=3
SE round, there are physical error
F_{3}
such that
\sigma(F_{3})=(0,1,0)
and measurement error
B_{3}=(0,1,0)
so that we observe syndrome
s_{3}=(0,0,0)
.
Recall that
s_{2}=\sigma(F_{2}D_{1})+B_{2}=(1,0,0)
, which means that the first syndrome bit is flipped from
t=2
to
t=3
, that is,
s_{2}+s_{3}=(1,0,0)
.

Let us now verify this using the syndrome change formula
\Delta_{3}=\sigma(F_{3})+B_{3}+B_{2}
which takes into account
new
error
F_{3}
between timestep
2
and
3
, as well as measurement errors
B_{2}
and
B_{3}
.
Since
D_{2}=F_{2}D_{1}
, we have

\displaystyle(1,0,0)=s_{2}+s_{3}=\Delta_{3}

\displaystyle=\sigma(F_{3})+B_{2}+B_{3}=(1,0,0)\,,

(481)

which indicates that we observe that the first syndrome bit is flipped.

Syndrome change
\Delta_{t}
provides information to the decoder about any errors between timestep
t
and
t-1
.
Up to the point after SE at timestep
t
is completed, the decoder have deduced errors
E_{1},E_{2},\dots,E_{t}
consistent with observed syndromes
s_{1},\dots,s_{t}
, namely

\begin{gathered}\sigma(F_{1})+B_{1}=s_{1}=\sigma(E_{1})+C_{1}\,,\\
\sigma(F_{2}F_{1})+B_{2}+B_{1}=s_{2}=\sigma(E_{2}E_{1})+C_{2}+C_{1}\,,\\
\vdots\\
\sigma(F_{t}\dots F_{1})+B_{t}+B_{t-1}=s_{t}=\sigma(E_{t}\dots E_{1})+C_{t}+C_{t-1}\,.\end{gathered}

(482)

Since
\sigma(F_{t}\dots F_{1})=\sigma(F_{t})+\sigma(F_{t-1}\dots F_{1})
and
\sigma(E_{t}\dots E_{1})=\sigma(E_{t})+\sigma(E_{t-1}\dots E_{1})
, we obtain a consistency relation between actual errors and deduced errors:

\begin{gathered}\sigma(F_{t})+B_{t}+B_{t-1}=\Delta_{t}=\sigma(E_{t})+C_{t}+C_{t-1}\quad,\;\forall t\geq 2\\
\text{and}\\
\sigma(F_{1})+B_{1}=\Delta_{1}=\sigma(E_{1})+C_{1}\,.\end{gathered}

(483)

Errors
E_{1},\dots,E_{T}
deduced by the decoders over the
T
SE cycles are the effective correction performed by the decoder.
So over the
T
SE cycles, the overall effect of both errors and corrections are given by
\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}
, where
E_{t}F_{t}
is the discrepancy between what the decoder thinks happened at round
t
, that is,
E_{t}
, and the actual error
F_{t}
.
Thus
\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}
is the overall discrepancy in the entire
T
-cycle SE circuit.
So, if the decoder deduced all errors accurately, that is,
E_{t}=F_{t}
, then there would be no discrepancy at the end of the SE cycles, that is,
\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}=\prod_{t=1}^{T}F_{t}F_{t}=I
.

Now note that by consistency condition in
Equation

483
, we have

\begin{gathered}\sigma(F_{t}E_{t})=\sigma(F_{t})+\sigma(E_{t})=B_{t}+B_{t-1}+C_{t}+C_{t-1}\quad,\;\forall t\geq 2\\
\text{and}\\
\sigma(F_{1}E_{1})=\sigma(F_{1})+\sigma(E_{1})=B_{1}+C_{1}\,.\end{gathered}

(484)

Suppose that we do a perfect syndrome measurement after cycle
T
(no measurement errors and no physical errors after cycle
T
).
This gives us syndrome

\displaystyle\sigma\Big(\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}\Big)

\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sigma(E_{t})+\sigma(F_{t})

(485)

\displaystyle=B_{1}+C_{1}+\sum_{t=2}^{T}B_{t}+B_{t-1}+C_{t}+C_{t-1}

\displaystyle=B_{T}+C_{T}

since there are pairs of
B_{t}
and
C_{t}
for all
t
in the summation which cancels out, except for
B_{T},C_{T}
.
With this syndrome the decoder will deduce a Pauli error
G
which is consistent with syndrome
\sigma(\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t})=B_{T}+C_{T}
and has minimum weight, that is,

G\in\arg\min\bigg\{{\mathrm{wt}}(G):\sigma(G)=\sigma\Big(\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}\Big)\bigg\}\,.

(486)

14.3.2
Syndrome adjacency graph and error clusters

Now that we have laid the groundwork for syndromes and syndrome errors, before proceeding to the main body of the proof for the error correction threshold of qLDPC codes with syndrome measurement errors, we need to define one more object to help us with relating qubit errors, syndrome errors, and the stabilizer checks.
Similar to the proof for a threshold for qLDPC codes with no measurement errors in
Section

14.2
, we will represent qubit errors and measurement bit-flip errors using a graph that take into consideration both data qubits and syndrome bits over
T
SE cycles.

{defbox}

[label=def:syndrome_adjacency_graph]Syndrome adjacency graph
For an
n
-qubit stabilizer code
Q
with stabilizer generators
g_{1},\dots,g_{l}
and a positive integer
T
, a simple graph
\Gamma
is the
syndrome adjacency graph
of
Q
over
T
SE cycles if its vertices
V(\Gamma)=X(\Gamma)\cup B(\Gamma)
and edges
E(\Gamma)=K(\Gamma)\cup L(\Gamma)
are given by

\begin{gathered}X(\Gamma)=\{(x,t):x\in[1,n],t\in[1,T+1]\}\quad,\\
B(\Gamma)=\{(b,t):b\in[1,l],t\in[1,T]\}\quad,\\
K(\Gamma)=\big\{((x,t),(y,t))\in X(\Gamma)\times X(\Gamma):\exists i\in[1,l],\;x,y\in{\mathrm{supp}}(g_{i})\big\}\quad,\\
L(\Gamma)=\big\{((b,t),(x,t^{\prime}))\in B(\Gamma)\times X(\Gamma):x\in{\mathrm{supp}}(g_{b}),\;t^{\prime}\in\{t,t+1\}\big\}\,.\end{gathered}

(487)

Namely, qubit vertices
X(\Gamma)
are labels for the
n
qubits at before and after each
T
SE cycles, syndrome vertices
B(\Gamma)
are labels of syndrome bits in each of the
T
SE cycles, edges
K(\Gamma)
connects any two qubits at timestep
t
involved in a stabilizer generator, and edges
L(\Gamma)
connects syndrome vertices at timestep
t
to qubit vertices at timestep
t
and
t+1
.

For an
(r,c)
-qLDPC code family
Q_{1},Q_{2},\dots
with parameters
\llbracket n_{1},k_{i},d_{i}\rrbracket
, each qubit vertex
(x,t)
is connected to at most other
r-1
qubit vertices at timestep
t
, connected to at most
c
syndrome vertices at timestep
t
, and to at most
c
syndrome vertices at timestep
t+1
.
So the degree of
(x,t)
is at most
2c+r-1
.
On the other hand, each syndrome vertex
(b,t)
is connected to at most
r
qubit vertices at timestep
t-1
and at most
r
qubit vertices at timestep
t
.
Thus, any syndrome vertex
(b,t)
has degree of at most
2r
.
So, a syndrome adjacency graph
\Gamma
corresponding to any code
Q_{i}
from an
(r,c)
-qLDPC code family
Q_{1},Q_{2},\dots
must have degree of at most
\max\{2c+r-1,2r\}
, which is a constant in
n_{i}
.

Now consider actual errors
F_{1},\dots,F_{T}
and
B_{1},\dots,B_{T}
, deduced errors
E_{1},\dots,E_{T}
and
C_{1},\dots,C_{T}
, and final correction
G
.
Then consider the following sets of “marked” vertices:

\begin{gathered}X_{\mathrm{mrk}}=\{(x,t)\in X(\Gamma):t\in[1,T]\,,\;(x,t)\in{\mathrm{supp}}(E_{t}F_{t})\}\,,\\
B_{\mathrm{mrk}}=\{(b,t)\in B(\Gamma):(B_{t}+C_{t})_{b}=1\}\,,\\
X_{\mathrm{mrk}}^{T+1}=\{(x,T+1)\in X(\Gamma):(x,T+1)\in{\mathrm{supp}}(G)\}\,.\end{gathered}

(488)

Namely, we mark qubit vertices
(x,t)\in X(\Gamma)
if qubit
x
at time
t\in\{1,\dots,T\}
is in the support of Pauli error
E_{t}F_{t}
, qubit vertices
(x,T+1)
at time
T+1
that are in the support of final correction Pauli
G
, and syndrome bit vertices
(b,t)
at time
t\in\{1,\dots,T\}
that are in the support of
B_{t}+C_{t}
.
For the rest of the proof, we will look into largest subsets of marked vertices from
V_{\mathrm{mrk}}=X_{\mathrm{mrk}}\cup B_{\mathrm{mrk}}\cup X_{\mathrm{mrk}}^{t+1}
that induces a connected subgraph which we call a
cluster
.
More precisely,
K\subseteq V_{\mathrm{mrk}}
is a cluster if (1) for all pairs of vertices
u,v\in K
there exist a sequence of edges
(u,w_{1}),(w_{1},w_{2}),\dots,(w_{l},v)
such that
w_{1},\dots,w_{l}\in K
and (2) for all vertices
v\in K
, all marked neighbors of
v
are
K
.
As an illustration, consider the following example.

Example 14.5

(label=ex:syndrome_adj_graph_clusters)
.

F
and final correction
G
:

Its syndrome adjacency graph is given by:

14.3.3
Properties of error clusters

As we discussed above, a cluster is a connected induced graph of the syndrome adjacency graph
\Gamma
consisting of marked nodes determined by qubit errors
F=F_{1},\dots,F_{T}
, syndrome errors
B=B_{1},\dots,B_{T}
, and the errors
(E=E_{1},\dots,E_{T},\;C=C_{1},\dots,C_{T},\;G)
deduced by the decoder throughout the circuit.
Clusters in
\Gamma
capture how all errors affect the final residual error
P=G\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}
at the end of the circuit, which determines whether the decoding is successful.
In the following, we will show properties of clusters in a series of lemmas that we use later to characterize logical errors and bound logical error rates to obtain thresholds.
First, we show that the residual error
P_{K}
caused by errors in cluster
K
must have a trivial syndrome.

{lembox}

[label=lem:connected_cluster_trivial_syndrome]Connected cluster trivial syndrome
For a connected cluster
K
, let
P_{K}=G|_{K}\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K}
where
F
is the actual errors,
E
the deduced errors,
G
the final correction, and
E|_{K}
is the restriction of Pauli
E
to
K
.
Then
\sigma(P_{K})=0
, that is, it has a trivial syndrome.

Proof 14.6
.

Recall that for all bits
b\in\{1,\dots,l\}
we have the consistency condition

\begin{gathered}\sigma(E_{t}F_{t})_{b}=(B_{t-1}+B_{t}+C_{t-1}+C_{t})_{b}\,,\;\forall t\in[2,T]\\
\text{and}\\
\sigma(E_{1}F_{1})_{b}=(B_{1}+C_{1})_{b}\,,\end{gathered}

(490)

by
Equation

484
.
Let us write
E_{t}=E_{t}|_{K}E_{t}|_{K^{\prime}}
and
F_{t}=F_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K^{\prime}}
where
K^{\prime}
is the complement of cluster
K
, so that the consistency conditions become

\begin{gathered}\sigma(E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K})_{b}+\sigma(E_{t}|_{K^{\prime}}F_{t}|_{K^{\prime}})_{b}=(B_{t-1}+C_{t-1})_{b}+(B_{t}+C_{t})_{b}\,,\;\forall t\in[2,T]\\
\text{and}\\
\sigma(E_{1}|_{K}F_{1}|_{K})_{b}+\sigma(E_{1}|_{K^{\prime}}F_{1}|_{K^{\prime}})_{b}=(B_{1}+C_{1})_{b}\,.\end{gathered}

(491)

By the definition of a cluster, all marked qubit vertices
(x,t)
and
(x,t+1)
in
K^{\prime}
for any qubit
x\in[n_{i}]
are not adjacent to syndrome bit vertex
(b,t)\in K
since all marked qubit vertices adjacent to
(b,t)
must be in
K
.
Namely, errors
E_{t}|_{K^{\prime}}F_{t}|_{K^{\prime}}
and
E_{t+1}|_{K^{\prime}}F_{t+1}|_{K^{\prime}}
are not in the support of stabilizer generator
g_{b}
and therefore must have trivial
b\textsuperscript{th}
syndrome:
\sigma(E_{t}|_{K^{\prime}}F_{t}|_{K^{\prime}})_{b}=\sigma(E_{t+1}|_{K^{\prime}}F_{t+1}|_{K^{\prime}})_{b}=0
.
Similarly, for
(b,t)\in K^{\prime}
errors
E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K}
and
E_{t+1}|_{K}F_{t+1}|_{K}
are not in the support of stabilizer generator
g_{b}
, thus its
b\textsuperscript{th}
syndrome is trivial.
Thus, for all
b\in[l]
,

\begin{gathered}(b,t)\in K\Rightarrow\sigma(E_{t}|_{K^{\prime}}F_{t}|_{K^{\prime}})_{b}=\sigma(E_{t+1}|_{K^{\prime}}F_{t+1}|_{K^{\prime}})_{b}=0\\
\quad\text{and}\quad\\
(b,t)\in K^{\prime}\Rightarrow\sigma(E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K})_{b}=\sigma(E_{t+1}|_{K}F_{t+1}|_{K})_{b}=0\,.\end{gathered}

(492)

Therefore, for
(b,t)\in K
, consistency conditions in
Equation

491
become

\begin{gathered}\sigma(E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K})_{b}=\begin{cases}(B_{t-1}+C_{t-1})_{b}+(B_{t}+C_{t})_{b}\quad&,\;\text{if }(b,t),(b,t-1)\in K\\
0\quad&,\;\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\,,\;\forall t\in[2,T]\\
\text{and}\\
\sigma(E_{1}|_{K}F_{1}|_{K})_{b}=\begin{cases}(B_{1}+C_{1})_{b}\quad&,\;\text{if }(b,1)\in K\\
0\quad&,\;\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\end{gathered}

(493)

Thus, the syndrome of the total physical errors from timestep
1
to
T
is

\sigma\Big(\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K}\Big)_{b}=\begin{cases}(B_{T}+C_{T})_{b}\quad&,\;\text{if }(b,T)\in K\\
0\quad&,\;\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

(494)

Similarly, for timestep
T+1
, errors
G|_{K^{\prime}}
are not in the support of stabilizer
g_{b}
for all
(b,T)\in K
and errors
G|_{K}
are not in the support of stabilizer
g_{b^{\prime}}
for all
(b^{\prime},T)\in K^{\prime}
so that

\begin{gathered}(b,T)\in K\Rightarrow\sigma(G|_{K^{\prime}})_{b}=0\quad\text{and}\quad(b^{\prime},T)\in K^{\prime}\Rightarrow\sigma(G|_{K})_{b^{\prime}}=0\,,\end{gathered}

(495)

which implies that

\sigma(G|_{K})_{b}=\begin{cases}(B_{T}+C_{T})_{b}\;&,\quad\text{if }(b,T)\in K\\
0\;&,\quad\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

(496)

So, it holds that

\displaystyle\sigma(P_{K})=\sigma\Big(G|_{K}\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K}\Big)

\displaystyle=\sigma(G|_{K})+\sigma\Big(\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K}\Big)=0\,,

(497)

which completes the proof.

The lemma above shows that errors
P_{K}=G|_{K}\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K}
in a cluster
K
do not trigger a syndrome flip.
In other words, if we can decompose
P
into clusters
K_{1},\dots,K_{m}
, then
\sigma(K_{i})=0
for all
i\in[m]
, and from the proof of
, this is due to any two nodes
(\xi,\tau)\in K_{i}
and
(\zeta,\tau^{\prime})\in K_{j}
for
j\neq i
must not share an edge and therefore cannot trigger the same syndrome check
(b,t)
.

The syndrome triviality of
P_{K}
could mean two things: (1)
P_{K}
is a non-trivial logical error or (2)
P_{K}
is a stabilizer.
The following lemma shows that if the residual error
P=G\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}
at the end of the
T
cycles is a non-trivial logical operator (thus resulting in a logical error), then there is a cluster
K
which contains errors
P_{K}
which itself is a logical operator and therefore has weight of at least the distance
d
of the code.

{lembox}

[label=lem:error_weight_lower_bound_decoding_failure]Error weight lower bound
If
P=G\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}
is a non-trivial logical operator of qLDPC code
Q
with stabilizer group
\mathcal{S}
and parameter
\llbracket n,k,d\rrbracket
(i.e.,
P\in\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{S})\setminus\mathcal{S}
), then there exists a cluster
K
such that
{\mathrm{wt}}(P_{K})\geq d
for
P_{K}=G|_{K}\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K}
.

Proof 14.7
.

Let
H=\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}
so that
P=GH
and assume that it is a non-trivial logical operator, that is,
GH\in\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{S})\setminus\mathcal{S}
.
We will then show that
P_{K}
is in
\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{S})\setminus\mathcal{S}
for at least one cluster
K
of
P
, that is, it is a logical operator.

Consider clusters
K_{1},\dots,K_{m}
of
P
so that
P=\prod_{i=1}^{m}P_{K_{i}}
.
By
, for each
i\in[m]
we have
\sigma(P_{K_{i}})=0
so that
P_{K_{i}}\in\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{S})
.
Now, assume that
P_{K_{i}}\in\mathcal{S}
for all
i\in[m]
.
Then this means that
P=\prod_{i=1}^{m}P_{K_{i}}\in\mathcal{S}
, which contradicts the assumption that
GH\in\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{S})\setminus\mathcal{S}
.
So,
P_{K}\in\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{S})\setminus\mathcal{S}
must hold.
All non-trivial logical operator of
Q
must have weight of at least
d
.
So,
{\mathrm{wt}}(P_{K})\geq d
.

By how we set our decoder, it chooses minimum weight Paulis that are consistent with the observed syndrome (c.f. consistency conditions in
Equation

483
).
Now we show that the minimum weight property of deduced errors restricted to any cluster
K
also holds.

{lembox}

[label=lem:total_error_weight_inequality]Total error weight
Consider cluster
K
and minimum weight deduced errors

\{E_{1},C_{1},\dots,E_{T},C_{T}\}\in\arg\min{\mathrm{wt}}(E,C)\,,

(498)

where
{\mathrm{wt}}(E,C)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(E_{t})+{\mathrm{wt}}(C_{t})
and the minimization is over errors
\{E_{t},C_{t}:t\in[T]\}
satisfying consistency constraints in
Equation

483
.
Then, it holds that

\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(E_{t}|_{K})+{\mathrm{wt}}(C_{t}|_{K})\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(F_{t}|_{K})+{\mathrm{wt}}(B_{t}|_{K})\,,

(499)

where
E_{t}|_{K}
is the errors at timestep
t
restricted to cluster
K
.

Proof 14.8
.

Consider a cluster
K
and its complement
K^{\prime}
and (not necessarily minimum weight) deduced errors
E_{1}^{\prime},C_{1}^{\prime},\dots,E_{T}^{\prime},C_{T}^{\prime}
such that

\begin{gathered}E_{t}^{\prime}|_{K}=F_{t}|_{K}\,,\quad C_{t}^{\prime}|_{K}=B_{t}|_{K}\,,\quad E_{t}^{\prime}|_{K^{\prime}}=E_{t}|_{K}\,,\;\text{and}\quad C_{t}^{\prime}|_{K^{\prime}}=C_{t}|_{K}\,.\end{gathered}

(500)

Namely,
(E^{\prime},C^{\prime})
are equal to actual errors
(F,B)
in cluster
K
, but equal to minimum weight deduced errors
(E,C)
in
K^{\prime}
.
Note that
E_{1}^{\prime},C_{1}^{\prime},\dots,E_{T}^{\prime},C_{T}^{\prime}
satisfy the constraints in
Equation

483
since for
t\geq 2

\begin{gathered}\sigma(E_{t}^{\prime}|_{K})+C_{t}^{\prime}|_{K}+C_{t-1}^{\prime}|_{K}=\sigma(F_{t}|_{K})+B_{t}|_{K}+B_{t-1}|_{K}\quad,\\
\sigma(E_{t}^{\prime}|_{K^{\prime}})+C_{t}^{\prime}|_{K^{\prime}}+C_{t-1}^{\prime}|_{K^{\prime}}=\sigma(E_{t}|_{K^{\prime}})+C_{t}|_{K^{\prime}}+C_{t-1}|_{K^{\prime}}=\sigma(F_{t}|_{K^{\prime}})+B_{t}|_{K^{\prime}}+B_{t-1}|_{K^{\prime}}\,,\\
\text{and}\\
\sigma(E_{1}^{\prime}|_{K})+C_{1}^{\prime}|_{K}=\sigma(F_{1}|_{K})+B_{1}|_{K}\quad,\\
\sigma(E_{1}^{\prime}|_{K^{\prime}})+C_{1}^{\prime}|_{K^{\prime}}=\sigma(E_{1}|_{K})+C_{1}|_{K}=\sigma(F_{1}|_{K^{\prime}})+B_{1}|_{K^{\prime}}\,.\end{gathered}

(501)

(See the proof of
.)
Since
{\mathrm{wt}}(E_{t}^{\prime}|_{K^{\prime}})+{\mathrm{wt}}(C_{t}^{\prime}|_{K^{\prime}})={\mathrm{wt}}(E_{t}|_{K^{\prime}})+{\mathrm{wt}}(C_{t}|_{K^{\prime}})
and
{\mathrm{wt}}(E_{t}^{\prime}|_{K^{\prime}})+{\mathrm{wt}}(C_{t}^{\prime}|_{K^{\prime}})={\mathrm{wt}}(F_{t}|_{K^{\prime}})+{\mathrm{wt}}(B_{t}|_{K^{\prime}})
, then we have

\begin{gathered}{\mathrm{wt}}(E^{\prime},C^{\prime})-{\mathrm{wt}}(E,C)=\bigg(\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(F_{t}|_{K})+{\mathrm{wt}}(B_{t}|_{K})\bigg)-\bigg(\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(E_{t}|_{K})+{\mathrm{wt}}(C_{t}|_{K})\bigg)\,.\end{gathered}

(502)

Since
E,C
are chosen as consistent errors with minimum weight, then
{\mathrm{wt}}(E^{\prime},C^{\prime})\geq{\mathrm{wt}}(E,C)
must hold.
Thus
Equation

499
holds.

Recall that clusters are defined by both the actual (qubit and syndrome) errors
F,B
as well as the errors
E,C,G
deduced by the decoders.
As such, it is not clear how many of the actual errors occurred in a cluster.
In the following lemma, we show that the total number of actual errors
F,B
in each cluster
K
must be either at least half of the size of
K
, or at least a quarter od the size of
K
.

{lembox}

[label=lem:cluster_faults_lower_bound]Cluster faults lower bound
Consider a cluster
K
with respect to qubit errors
E_{1}F_{1},\dots,E_{T}F_{T},G
and syndrome bit errors
B_{1},C_{1},\dots,B_{T},C_{T}
.
If
K
contains no vertices of the form
(x,T+1)
(i.e.,
G|_{K}=I
), then the number of faults
A_{K}
in cluster
K
satisfies

A_{K}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(F_{t}|_{K})+{\mathrm{wt}}(B_{t}|_{K})\geq\frac{|K|}{2}\,.

(503)

Also, if
K
contains at least one vertex of the form
(x,T+1)
(i.e.,
G|_{K}\neq I
), then

A_{K}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(F_{t}|_{K})+{\mathrm{wt}}(B_{t}|_{K})\geq\frac{|K|}{4}\,.

(504)

Proof 14.9
.

Consider the total weight of all deduced errors
D_{K}
, all qubit errors
U_{K}
, and all syndrome errors
V_{K}
in cluster
K
:

\begin{gathered}D_{K}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(E_{t}|_{K})+{\mathrm{wt}}(C_{t}|_{K})\,,\quad U_{K}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(F_{t}|_{K})+{\mathrm{wt}}(E_{t}|_{K})\,,\\
\text{and}\quad V_{K}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(B_{t}|_{K})+{\mathrm{wt}}(C_{t}|_{K})\,.\end{gathered}

(505)

Now recall that each qubit node
(q,t)
for
1\leq t\leq T
is marked if qubit
q
is in the support of
E_{t}F_{t}
, each syndrome bit node
(b,t)
is marked if the
b\textsuperscript{th}
bit of
B_{t}+C_{t}
is 1, and each qubit node
(q,T+1)
is marked if
G|_{q}\neq I
.
Denote the number of marked qubits in
K
from timestep
1
to
T
by
s_{q}
, the number of marked syndrome bits in
K
by
s_{c}
, and the number of marked qubits in
T+1
by
s_{g}={\mathrm{wt}}(G|_{K})
, so that
|K|=s_{c}+s_{q}+s_{g}
.

First we will show that
A_{K}\geq|K|/2
assuming that
G|_{K}=I
(so,
s_{g}=0
).
Note that
U_{K}\geq s_{q}
since for each qubit node
(q,t)\in K
either
E_{t}|_{q}\neq I
or
F_{t}|_{q}\neq I
.
Similarly, we have
V_{K}\geq s_{q}
since for each syndrome bit node
(b,t)\in K
either
C_{t}|_{q}=1
or
B_{t}|_{q}=1
.
Then, we have

A_{K}+D_{K}=U_{K}+V_{K}\geq s_{c}+s_{q}=|K|\,.

(506)

By
, it holds that
D_{K}\leq A_{K}
.
So, we obtain

|K|\leq A_{K}+D_{K}\leq 2A_{K}\,.

(507)

which implies that
A_{K}\geq|K|/2
as claimed.

Now we will show that
A_{K}\geq|K|/4
if
G|_{K}\neq I
.
We will first show an upper bound to the number of vertices in
G|_{K}
as
s_{g}={\mathrm{wt}}(G|_{K})\leq U_{K}
.
First note that
\sigma(G)=B_{T}+C_{T}=\sigma(\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t})
by the definition of correction
G
.
This is true for all the errors and correction restricted to
K
, that is,
\sigma(G|_{K})=B_{T}|_{K}+C_{T}|_{K}=\sigma(\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K})
since
\sigma(G|_{K})_{b}=(B_{T}|_{K}+C_{T}|_{K})_{b}
whenever
(b,T)\in K
and
\sigma(G|_{K})_{b}=0
otherwise as all marked qubit nodes
(q,T+1)
adjacent to a
(b,T)\in K
must be in
K
.
By a similar argument,
\sigma(\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K})_{b}=(B_{T}|_{K}+C_{T}|_{K})_{b}
whenever
(b,T)\in K
and
\sigma(\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K})_{b}=0
otherwise.
(This is the same line of argument given in the proof of
).
Since
G
is chosen to be the smallest weight operator such that
\sigma(G)=\sigma(\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t})
, we have

s_{g}={\mathrm{wt}}(G|_{K})\leq{\mathrm{wt}}\Big(\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K}\Big)\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K})\leq U_{K}\,.

(508)

By the argument for the
G|_{K}=I
case above, we have
A_{K}+D_{K}\geq s_{c}+s_{q}
.
Then, since
|K|=s_{q}+s_{c}+s_{g}
and
U_{K}\leq A_{K}+D_{K}
we obtain

|K|\leq A_{K}+D_{K}+U_{K}\leq 2(A_{K}+D_{K})\,.

(509)

Since
D_{K}\leq A_{K}
.
By
, we have

|K|\leq 4A_{K}\,,

(510)

which implies that
A_{K}\geq|K|/4
, as claimed.

So far we have not considered the probability of a certain number of actual errors in a cluster.
We now show an upper bound to the probability of at least
m
actual errors (or, “faults”) in a cluster
K
(in fact we show this for any subset of vertices that are not necessarily connected).

{lembox}

[label=lem:faults_in_cluster_probability]Probability of faults in cluster
For a subset of vertices
U\subseteq V(\Gamma)
and local-stochastic noise model with error parameter
p_{*}
, it holds that

\Pr[\text{There are at least $m$ faults in $U$}\Big]\leq p_{*}^{m}2^{|U|}\,.

(511)

Proof 14.10
.

Note that by a union bound and by the definition of the local-stochastic noise model, we have

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{There are at least $m$ faults in $U$}\Big]

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{V\subseteq U:|V|\geq m}\Pr[\text{All qubits in $V$ are faulty}]

(512)

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{V\subseteq U:|V|\geq m}p_{*}^{m}\,.

There are
\binom{|U|}{k}
subsets of
U
with size
k
.
Thus,

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{There are at least $m$ faults in $U$}\Big]

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=m}^{|U|}\binom{|U|}{k}p_{*}^{k}

(513)

\displaystyle\leq p_{*}^{m}\sum_{k=m}^{|U|}\binom{|U|}{k}\leq p_{*}^{m}2^{|U|}\,,

since
\sum_{k=0}^{s}\binom{s}{k}=2^{s}
.

Now we show the last property of clusters in a graph.
This is the same property we used in the proof of decoding threshold without syndrome errors (c.f.
Equation

468
of
Section

14.2
), which uses Lemma 2 of
[
113
]
.

{lembox}

[label=lem:number_of_clusters_upper_bound]Upper bound on number of clusters
[
113
, Lemma 2]

For any graph
\Gamma
with maximum degree
z^{\prime}
, the number of connected clusters
K
of size
|K|=s
containing vertex
v\in V(\Gamma)
is at most
(z^{\prime}e)^{s-1}
and the total number of connected clusters of size
s
is at most
|V(\Gamma)|(z^{\prime}e)^{s-1}
.

Bounding logical error probability

Now we will bound the logical error rate that grows either as
O(nT(p^{\prime}/p_{i})^{d})
,
O(n(p^{\prime}/p_{f})^{d})
,
O(n(p^{\prime\prime}/p_{i})^{d})
, or
O(n(p^{\prime\prime}/p_{f})^{d})
, according to different types of clusters causing the logical error, for some
p_{i},p_{f}
and for
p^{\prime}=\max\{p,q\}
and
p^{\prime\prime}=\max\{\tilde{p},p,q\}
.
First, let us consider errors and corrections
G,E_{1},B_{1},\dots,E_{T},B_{T},F_{1},C_{1},\dots,F_{T},C_{T}
so that a decoding failure results in a logical error
P=G\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}\in\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{S})\setminus\mathcal{S}
, which restriction to a cluster
K
yields
P_{K}=G|_{K}\prod_{t=1}^{T}(E_{t}F_{t})|_{K}
, with actual number of faults
A_{K}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(F_{t}|_{K})+{\mathrm{wt}}(B_{t}|_{K})
.
By
, a logical error implies the existence of cluster
K
such that
{\mathrm{wt}}(P_{K})\geq d
, so that the size
|K|
of such “bad” cluster must satisfy
|K|\geq{\mathrm{wt}}(P_{K})\geq d
.
So, the probability of a logical error can be bounded as

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{Logical error}]

\displaystyle\leq\Pr[\text{There is a cluster $K$ s.t. ${\mathrm{wt}}(P_{K})\geq d$}]

(514)

\displaystyle\leq\Pr[\text{There is a cluster $K$ s.t. $|K|\geq d$}]

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{s\geq d}\Pr[\text{There is a cluster $K$ s.t. $|K|=s$}]\,.

Now, let us consider four types of logical errors according to the bad cluster
K
causing it:

1.

K
does not contain both initial errors and final errors (i.e.,
(E_{1}F_{1})|_{K}=I
and
G|_{K}=I
).

2.

K
does not contain any final errors but contains some initial errors (i.e.,
(E_{1}F_{1})|_{K}=I
and
G|_{K}\neq I
).

3.

K
does not contain any initial errors but contains some final errors (i.e.,
(E_{1}F_{1})|_{K}\neq I
and
G|_{K}=I
).

4.

K
contains both initial errors and final errors (i.e.,
(E_{1}F_{1})|_{K}\neq I
and
G|_{K}\neq I
).

By
, the number of faults
A_{K}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(F_{t}|_{K})+{\mathrm{wt}}(B_{t}|_{K})
in cluster
K
must satisfy

\begin{gathered}A_{K}\geq|K|/2\quad\text{if }G|_{K}=I\quad\text{and}\quad A_{K}\geq|K|/4\quad\text{if }G|_{K}\neq I\,,\end{gathered}

(515)

Then for a cluster
K
, we can use
to bound the probability of number of faults in
K
for each of these four cases as

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{At least $|K|/2$ faults in $K$}]\leq(p^{\prime})^{|K|/2}2^{|K|}

\displaystyle,\quad\text{if }(E_{1}F_{1})|_{K}=I\,,\;G|_{K}=I\,,

(516)

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{At least $|K|/4$ faults in $K$}]\leq(p^{\prime})^{|K|/4}2^{|K|}

\displaystyle,\quad\text{if }(E_{1}F_{1})|_{K}=I\,,\;G|_{K}\neq I\,,

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{At least $|K|/2$ faults in $K$}]\leq(p^{\prime\prime})^{|K|/2}2^{|K|}

\displaystyle,\quad\text{if }(E_{1}F_{1})|_{K}\neq I\,,\;G|_{K}=I\,,

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{At least $|K|/4$ faults in $K$}]\leq(p^{\prime\prime})^{|K|/4}2^{|K|}

\displaystyle,\quad\text{if }(E_{1}F_{1})|_{K}\neq I\,,\;G|_{K}\neq I\,,

for
p^{\prime}=\max\{p,q\}
and
p^{\prime\prime}=\max\{\tilde{p},p,q\}
.

For case 1, we only need to consider vertices contained from timestep
2
to
T
since the cluster
K
is contained in this interval.
Thus there are
nT
vertices that could be contained in such
K
, and by
there are at most
(nT)(z^{\prime}e)^{s-1}
such clusters of size
s
.
Hence,

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{Logical error type 1}]

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{s\geq d}\Pr[\exists\text{ a type 1 cluster $K$ s.t. $|K|=s$}]

(517)

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{K:|K|=s\geq d}(nT)(z^{\prime}e)^{s-1}\Pr[\text{At least $|K|/2$ faults in $K$}]

\displaystyle\leq\frac{nT}{z^{\prime}e}\sum_{s\geq d}(2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime}})^{s}\,.

Since
\sum_{a\geq d}c^{a}=a^{d}/(1-a)
for all
a<1
, if
2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime}}<1
we have

\Pr[\text{Logical error type 1}]\leq\frac{nT}{z^{\prime}e}\frac{(2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime}})^{d}}{1-2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime}}}\,.

(518)

Defining
p_{i}=(2z^{\prime}e)^{-2}
, we have

\Pr[\text{Logical error type 1}]\leq\frac{nT}{z^{\prime}e(1-2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime}})}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime}}{p_{i}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{2}}\,.

(519)

For case 2, the cluster
K
must contain at least one of the
n
qubits at timestep
T+1
.
So, by
there are at most
n(z^{\prime}e)^{s-1}
such clusters of size
s
.
Hence,

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{Logical error type 2}]

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{s\geq d}\Pr[\exists\text{ a type 2 cluster $K$ s.t. $|K|=s$}]

(520)

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{K:|K|=s\geq d}n(z^{\prime}e)^{s-1}\Pr[\text{At least $|K|/4$ faults in $K$}]

\displaystyle\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e}\sum_{s\geq d}(2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}})^{s}\,.

If
2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}}<1
, then we have

\Pr[\text{Logical error type 2}]\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e}\frac{(2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}})^{d}}{1-2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}}}\,.

(521)

Defining
p_{f}=(2z^{\prime}e)^{-4}
, we have

\Pr[\text{Logical error type 2}]\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e(1-2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}})}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime}}{p_{f}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{4}}\,.

(522)

For case 3, the cluster
K
must contain at least one of the
n
qubits at timestep
1
.
So, by
there are at most
n(z^{\prime}e)^{s-1}
such clusters of size
s
.
Hence,

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{Logical error type 3}]

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{s\geq d}\Pr[\exists\text{ a type 3 cluster $K$ s.t. $|K|=s$}]

(523)

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{K:|K|=s\geq d}n(z^{\prime}e)^{s-1}\Pr[\text{At least $|K|/2$ faults in $K$}]

\displaystyle\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e}\sum_{s\geq d}(2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime\prime}})^{s}\,.

If
2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime\prime}}<1
, then we have

\Pr[\text{Logical error type 3}]\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e}\frac{(2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime\prime}})^{d}}{1-2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime\prime}}}\,.

(524)

Thus, we can again use
p_{i}=(2z^{\prime}e)^{-2}
to obtain

\Pr[\text{Logical error type 3}]\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e(1-2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime\prime}})}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime\prime}}{p_{i}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{2}}\,.

(525)

For case 4, cluster
K
must contain at least
2T+1
vertices since it spans all qubits from timestep
1
to
T+1
as well as at least
T
syndrome bit vertices in between those
T+1
layers of qubit vertices, that is,
|K|\geq 2T+1
.
So, by
there are at most
(2T+1)(z^{\prime}e)^{s-1}
such clusters of size
s
.
Hence,

\displaystyle\Pr[\text{Logical error type 4}]

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{s\geq 2T+1}\Pr[\exists\text{ a type 4 cluster $K$ s.t. $|K|=s$}]

(526)

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{K:|K|=s\geq 2T+1}n(z^{\prime}e)^{s-1}\Pr[\text{At least $|K|/4$ faults in $K$}]

\displaystyle\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e}\sum_{s\geq 2T+1}(2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}})^{s}\,.

If
2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}}<1
, then we have

\Pr[\text{Logical error type 4}]\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e}\frac{(2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}})^{2T+1}}{1-2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}}}\,.

(527)

Thus, for
p_{f}=(2z^{\prime}e)^{-4}
, we have

\Pr[\text{Logical error type 4}]\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e(1-2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}})}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime\prime}}{p_{f}}\Big)^{\frac{1}{4}}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime\prime}}{p_{f}}\Big)^{\frac{T}{2}}\,.

(528)

To summarize, the probability of each type of logical errors is bounded as:

\begin{gathered}\Pr[\text{Logical error type 1}]\leq\frac{nT}{z^{\prime}e(1-2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime}})}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime}}{p_{i}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{2}}\,,\\
\Pr[\text{Logical error type 2}]\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e(1-2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}})}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime}}{p_{f}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{4}}\,,\\
\Pr[\text{Logical error type 3}]\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e(1-2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime\prime}})}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime\prime}}{p_{i}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{2}}\,,\\
\Pr[\text{Logical error type 4}]\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e(1-2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}})}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime\prime}}{p_{f}}\Big)^{\frac{1}{4}}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime\prime}}{p_{f}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{2}}\,,\end{gathered}

(529)

where we set the total number of timesteps as
T=d
for
p_{f}=(2z^{\prime}e)^{-4}
and
p_{i}=(2z^{\prime}e)^{-2}
.

14.3.4
Residual error rate

We now show that the remaining residual errors after
T
rounds of syndrome extraction are local stochastic when the decoding is successful.
Note that a successful decoding means that
G\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}
is in the stabilizer group
\mathcal{S}
, whereas decoding failure means that it is in
\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{S})\setminus\mathcal{S}
.
For an initial codestate
\rho
, the actual state after
T
syndrome extraction rounds with faults
F=F_{T}\dots F_{1}
and inferred errors
E=E_{T}\dots E_{1}
is

F\rho F^{\dagger}=\Big(E\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}\Big)\rho\Big(E\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}\Big)^{\dagger}=\Big(EG^{\dagger}G\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}\Big)\rho\Big(EG^{\dagger}G\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}\Big)^{\dagger}\,,

(530)

since
F=E\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}
(up to some phase).
If
G\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}\in\mathcal{S}
, then it acts trivially to codestate
\rho
and we obtain

F\rho F^{\dagger}=EG\rho GE\,.

(531)

Since
E
is the errors that the decoder has inferred throughout the
T
rounds, then the actual remaining residual error is
G
15
15

15

Here,
E
can be removed because it is the frame that is applied in software (not a gate that is actually performed) to the codestate once it is inferred by the decoder.
. Since
G
is the residual error that will act as an initial error in the next SE cycle, we need to determine its error rate.

If the decoding results in no logical error and there is no cluster spanning from timestep
1
to
T+1
, then the correction operator
G
is local stochastic (c.f.
) over the output
n
qubits with error rate
p_{0}/3
for some
p_{0}\in(0,1)
if qubit error rate
p
and syndrome bit error rate
q
are small enough.
Namely, if
G\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}F_{t}\notin\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{S})\setminus\mathcal{S}
and
G|_{K}=I
or
E|_{1}F|_{1}=I
, then the probability of errors on output qubits
S
is

\Pr[\text{errors }S\subseteq{\mathrm{supp}}(G)\Big]\leq(p_{0}/3)^{|S|}\,,

(532)

whenever
p_{0}>3(4z^{\prime}e^{2}\sqrt{p^{\prime}})
and
e(1-2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{1/4})\geq 1
, where
p^{\prime}=\max\{p,q\}
.

Consider a subset
S
of the
n
qubits at timestep
T+1
of size
|S|=a
.
Then consider all clusters
K_{1},K_{2},\dots,K_{m}
intersecting
S
from
E_{1}F_{1},\dots,E_{T}F_{T},G
, that is, all clusters
K_{j}
such that
K_{j}\cap S\neq\emptyset
and
(\bigcup_{j}K_{j})|_{T+1}=S\subseteq{\mathrm{supp}}(G)
.
Now let
s_{j,q}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(E_{t}|_{K_{j}}F_{t}|_{K_{j}})
be the number of marked qubit vertices from timestep
1
to
T
in cluster
K_{j}
and
s_{j,c}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(B_{t}|_{K_{j}}C_{t}|_{K_{j}})
the marked syndrome vertices and
s_{j,g}={\mathrm{wt}}(G|_{K_{j}})
the marked qubit vertices at timestep
T+1
.
So, the size of each such cluster is
|K_{j}|=s_{j,q}+s_{j,c}+s_{j,g}
and the total size of all clusters
K_{1},\dots,K_{m}
intersecting
S
is

s=\sum_{j=1}^{m}s_{j,q}+s_{j,c}+s_{j,g}\,,

(533)

since all clusters are disjoint.

Now note that the total size of output qubits in clusters intersecting
S
is
\sum_{j}s_{j,g}=a
.
Since
G|_{K}
is a minimum-weight error with syndrome
\sigma(G|_{K})=B_{T}|_{K}+C_{T}|_{K}=\sigma(\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K})
, we have

{\mathrm{wt}}(G|_{K})\leq{\mathrm{wt}}\Big(\prod_{t=1}^{T}E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K}\Big)\leq\sum_{t=1}^{K}{\mathrm{wt}}(E_{t}|_{K}F_{t}|_{K})

(534)

by the same argument as given in the proof of
.
Thus for the clusters intersecting
S
we have
s_{j,g}\leq s_{j,q}
, and therefore the total size of the union of clusters
K_{1},\dots,K_{m}
is lower bounded as

\displaystyle s=\sum_{j=1}^{m}s_{j,q}+s_{j,c}+s_{j,g}\geq\sum_{j=1}^{m}2s_{j,g}\geq 2a\,.

(535)

Now, since all clusters
K_{1},\dots,K_{m}
intersecting
S
has some vertices in timestep
T+1
in it, by
the total number of actual faults
A_{j}
in each cluster
K_{j}
is lower bounded as

A_{j}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{wt}}(F_{t}|_{K_{j}})+{\mathrm{wt}}(B_{t}|_{K_{j}})\geq\frac{|K_{j}|}{4}\,.

(536)

Thus the total number of actual faults in the union of clusters
K_{1},\dots,K_{m}
is lower bounded as

\sum_{j=1}^{m}A_{j}\geq\frac{1}{4}\sum_{j=1}^{m}|K_{j}|=\frac{s}{4}\,.

(537)

So, by
the probability of at least
s/4
faults in
K_{1},\dots,K_{m}
is

\Pr[s/4\text{ faults in }K_{1},\dots,K_{m}]\leq p^{s/4}2^{s}\,.

(538)

By Lemma 2 of
[
113
]
, the number of sets
U
of size
s
that are a union of connected clusters in a graph
\Gamma
with maximum degree
z^{\prime}
such that
U
contains a subset of vertices
S
of size
|S|=a
is upper-bounded by
e^{a-1}(z^{\prime}e)^{s-a}
.
Thus, the probability of clusters
K_{1},\dots,K_{m}
such that sets
(\bigcup_{j}K_{j})|_{T+1}=S
such that
|S|=a
, given that the decoding succeeded, is upper-bounded as

\displaystyle\Pr[\Big(\bigcup_{j}K_{j}\Big)|_{T+1}=S\,,\;S\subseteq{\mathrm{supp}}(G)\,,\;|S|=a]

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{s\geq 2a}e^{a-1}(z^{\prime}e)^{s-a}(p^{\prime})^{s/4}2^{s}

(539)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{e(z^{\prime})^{a}}\sum_{s\geq 2a}(2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}})^{s}\,,

since the total size
s=\sum_{j}|K_{j}|
of clusters
K_{1},K_{2},\dots
must be at least
2a
by
Equation

535
and the total number of actual faults across them must be at least
s/4
by
Equation

537
.
Note that we use
p^{\prime}=\max\{p,q\}
, which is the maximum between qubit error rate
p
and syndrome error rate
q
, since we assume that clusters with support from timestep 1 to
T+1
is considered as a decoding failure.
Since we only consider all clusters containing some output qubit vertices, these clusters cannot contain initial qubits if we assume that the decoding succeeded.
Lastly, if
2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}}<1
then we can use the geometric sum identity
\sum_{s\geq t}c^{s}=\frac{c^{t}}{1-c}
for
c<1
to obtain

\displaystyle\Pr[\Big(\bigcup_{j}K_{j}\Big)|_{T+1}=S\subseteq{\mathrm{supp}}(G)]

\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{e(z^{\prime})^{|S|}}\frac{(2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{1/4})^{2|S|}}{(1-2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{1/4})}

(540)

\displaystyle=\frac{(4z^{\prime}e^{2}\sqrt{p^{\prime}})^{|S|}}{e(1-2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{1/4})}\,.

Thus if
p_{0}>3(4z^{\prime}e^{2}\sqrt{p^{\prime}})
and
e(1-2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{1/4})\geq 1
, then we have

\Pr[S\subseteq{\mathrm{supp}}(G)]\leq\Big(\frac{p_{0}}{3}\Big)^{|S|}\,,

(541)

which means that output error
G
is local stochastic with rate
p_{0}/3
.

14.3.5
Bounding logical error rates

Lastly let us pick the thresholds
p_{0},p_{1},p_{2}
for the initial errors
\tilde{p}
, qubit SE errors
p
, and syndrome bit errors
q
, respectively, so that the local-stochastic output error in
Equation

532
is satisfied and the logical error rates in
Equation

529
are bounded by functions exponential in code distance
d
.

First, recall the logical error probability bounds for the four different types of errors given in
Equation

529
:

\begin{gathered}\Pr[\text{Logical error type 1}]\leq\frac{nT}{z^{\prime}e(1-2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime}})}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime}}{p_{f}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{2}}\,,\\
\Pr[\text{Logical error type 2}]\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e(1-2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}})}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime}}{p_{f}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{4}}\,,\\
\Pr[\text{Logical error type 3}]\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e(1-2z^{\prime}e\sqrt{p^{\prime\prime}})}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime\prime}}{p_{f}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{2}}\,,\\
\Pr[\text{Logical error type 4}]\leq\frac{n}{z^{\prime}e(1-2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime\prime})^{\frac{1}{4}})}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime\prime}}{p_{f}}\Big)^{\frac{1}{4}}\Big(\frac{p^{\prime\prime}}{p_{f}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{2}}\end{gathered}

(542)

for
p^{\prime}=\max\{p,q\}
and
p^{\prime\prime}=\max\{\tilde{p},p,q\}
and
p_{f}=(2z^{\prime}e)^{-4}

16
16

16

Note that we use
p_{f}
for all the bounds, since the bounds in
Equation

529
with
p_{i}=(2z^{\prime}e)^{-2}
is stricter compared to ones with
p_{f}<p_{i}
).

.
Let us set our first threshold
p_{0}
as
p_{0}=p_{f}=(2z^{\prime}e)^{-4}
.

In the output error rate analysis above, we need
p^{\prime}=\max\{p,q\}
to be small enough such that
p_{0}>3(4z^{\prime}e^{2}\sqrt{p^{\prime}})
and
e(1-2z^{\prime}e(p^{\prime})^{1/4})\geq 1
.
So,

p^{\prime}\leq\min\Big\{\Big(\frac{p_{0}}{3(4z^{\prime}e^{2}\sqrt{p^{\prime}})}\Big)^{2},\Big(\frac{e-1}{2z^{\prime}e}\Big)^{4}\Big\}\,.

(543)

Thus, we need to set threshold
p_{1}
and
p_{2}
so that
p\leq p_{1}
and
q\leq p_{2}
, such that the upper bound on
p^{\prime}
holds.
This can be satisfied by setting

p_{1}=p_{2}=\frac{p_{f}^{2}}{144(z^{\prime})^{2}e^{4}}=(192(z^{\prime})^{5}e^{6})^{-2}\,.

(544)

Thus whenever
\tilde{p}<p_{0}
,
p<p_{1}
, and
q<p_{2}
, the logical error rates are bounded as

\begin{gathered}\Pr[\text{Logical error type 1}]\leq O\Big(nT\Big(\frac{p^{\prime}}{p_{0}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{2}}\Big)\,,\\
\Pr[\text{Logical error type 2}]\leq O\Big(n\Big(\frac{p^{\prime}}{p_{0}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{4}}\Big)\,,\\
\Pr[\text{Logical error type 3}]\leq O\Big(n\Big(\frac{p^{\prime\prime}}{p_{0}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{2}}\Big)\,,\\
\Pr[\text{Logical error type 4}]\leq O\Big(n\Big(\frac{p^{\prime\prime}}{p_{0}}\Big)^{\frac{d}{2}}\Big)\,.\end{gathered}

(545)

14.4
Threshold theorem for constant-overhead FTQC scheme

Gottesman’s FT scheme
[
113
]
simulates logical quantum circuit
C
with
k
qubits and
f(k)

locations
using
O(k)
physical qubits at any given time and
O(f(k){\textrm{poly}\,}k)
circuit locations.
Namely, this scheme has a constant
\frac{O(k)}{k}=O(1)
space overhead and polynomial
\frac{O(f(k){\textrm{poly}\,}k)}{f(k)}=O({\textrm{poly}\,}k)
time overhead.
For simplicity, we also assume that the circuit
C
consists of Clifford gates
\{{{H}},{\mathrm{CNOT}},{{S}}\}
and a non-Clifford gate
{{T}}
.

The code family
\{Q_{i}\}
with parameters
\llbracket n_{i},k_{i},d_{i}\rrbracket
used in the scheme is
(r,c)
-LDPC: each stabilizer generator acts on at most
r
qubits and each qubit involved in at most
c
generators, for constants
r,c
independent of
i
.
Moreover, we also demand some additional properties of the code family:

1.

Encoding rate
R=\lim_{i\rightarrow\infty}k_{i}/n_{i}>0
.

2.

Distance
d_{i}\to\infty
.

3.

Growth of number of physical qubits:
0<n_{i}-n_{i-1}<n_{i-1}^{\beta}
for
\beta>0
.

4.

If thresholds
\tilde{p}<p_{0}
,
p<p_{1}
, and
q<p_{2}
are satisfied and
T(n_{i})
SE rounds are performed, then the code is decodable with logical error rate
p_{L}=O(1/g(n_{i}))
, for
g(n)=\Omega({\textrm{poly}\,}n)
and
T(n)={\textrm{poly}\,}n
.

Other than the qLDPC code family, below we list key ingredients and ideas that go into this FTQC scheme, each of which we discuss in detail:

1.

Block-encode
k
logical qubits into
M=\lceil\frac{k}{k_{i}}\rceil
blocks of
(r,c)
-qLDPC codes
Q_{i}
satisfying the conditions above (for an illustration comparing this block encoding scheme to the concatenated code encoding in
Section

13
, see
Figure

26
).

2.

Sequential FT circuit
: one logical operation at a time.

3.

Cycle error correction (EC) across
M
blocks of
Q_{i}
, sharing ancillas.

4.

Shor-style syndrome extraction (SE)
with cat-state ancillas.

5.

Knill-style teleportation
for logical gates and measurements with offline ancilla preparation using concatenated codes.

First, though, we discuss the fault tolerance and noise model used for the scheme.

Figure 26:
Illustration of encoding by concatenation (left) and block encoding (right).
In both figures, blue circles represent physical qubits and green circles represent logical qubits.
On the left-hand side, each green circle represent an outer
\llbracket 4,1\rrbracket
code, where each one of its four qubits (yellow, rounded squares) is itself a
\llbracket 4,1\rrbracket
code (where the four physical qubits are the blue circles inside a yellow rounded square).
Thus, the 12 logical qubits use
12\times 16=192
physical qubits through two levels of concatenation.
On the right-hand side, each red, rounded rectangle is a
\llbracket 16,3\rrbracket
code, where the 16 physical qubits are represented by blue circles and the 3 logical qubits by green circles.
Thus, with 4 copies of the
\llbracket 16,3\rrbracket
code, we can encode 12 logical qubits using
4\times 16=64
physical qubits.

14.4.1
Basic model and simplified model of fault tolerance

Here we adopt the
basic model of fault tolerance
.
In this model, we consider locations of a circuit
C
, denoted by
{\texttt{loc}}(C)
, as the set of all potentially faulty components, which includes state preparation, gates, measurements, and wait locations.
For example, consider the following circuit with two state preparation locations, one single-qubit gate location, one two-qubit gate location, one measurement location, and two wait locations:

\quantikz\gate[1,style={blue!0,fill=blue!0,fillopacity=0,opacity=0}]{|0\rangle}\gategroup[1,steps=1,style={roundedcorners,dashed,fillopacity=0,innerxsep=0.3pt,innerysep=0.3pt},background,labelstyle={labelposition=above,anchor=north,yshift=0.3cm}]{{\footnotesize prep}}&\gate[1]{{{H}}}\gategroup[1,steps=1,style={roundedcorners,dashed,fillopacity=0,innerxsep=0.3pt,innerysep=0.3pt},background,labelstyle={labelposition=above,anchor=north,yshift=0.3cm}]{{\footnotesize 1-qgate}}\ctrl{1}\gategroup[2,steps=1,style={roundedcorners,dashed,fillopacity=0,innerxsep=0.3pt,innerysep=0.3pt},background,labelstyle={labelposition=below,anchor=north,yshift=-0.2cm}]{{\footnotesize 2-qgate}}\meter{}\gategroup[1,steps=1,style={roundedcorners,dashed,fillopacity=0,innerxsep=0.3pt,innerysep=0.3pt},background,labelstyle={labelposition=above,anchor=north,yshift=0.3cm}]{{\footnotesize meas.}}\\
\gate[1,style={blue!0,fill=blue!0,fillopacity=0,opacity=0}]{|0\rangle}\gategroup[1,steps=1,style={roundedcorners,dashed,fillopacity=0,innerxsep=0.3pt,innerysep=0.3pt},background,labelstyle={labelposition=below,anchor=north,yshift=-0.3cm}]{{\footnotesize prep}}\gategroup[1,steps=1,style={roundedcorners,dashed,fillopacity=0,innerxsep=0.3pt,innerysep=0.3pt},background,labelstyle={labelposition=below,anchor=north,yshift=0.3cm}]{{\footnotesize wait}}\targ{}\gategroup[1,steps=1,style={roundedcorners,dashed,fillopacity=0,innerxsep=0.3pt,innerysep=0.3pt},background,labelstyle={labelposition=below,anchor=north,yshift=0.3cm}]{{\footnotesize wait}}

(546)

We adopt the local stochastic noise model as defined in
so that for an error rate
p
, the probability of faults in a subset of locations
S\subseteq{\texttt{loc}}(C)
is at most
p^{|S|}
.

Later, for the fault tolerance analysis of the error correction cycles, we will instead use a
simplified model of fault tolerance
.
In the simplified model, we instead consider three different types of faults with local-stochastic noise: initial input errors with rate
\tilde{p}
, output data qubit errors with rate
p_{D}
, and syndrome bit-flip errors with rate
q
.
Note that this is the model that we use in the qLDPC code decoding threshold in
Section

14.3
.
To illustrate this more concretely and to compare between the basic model and simplified model of fault tolerance in syndrome extraction circuits, consider the following
T
iterations of a generic syndrome extraction circuit in the basic model:

\quantikz[rowsep=0.5cm,columnsep=0.5cm,classicalgap=0.05cm]\setwiretype{n}\slice{}&\gate[style={red!20,fill=red!20}]{|\text{anc}\rangle}\ctrl{1}\setwiretype{b}\gate[style={fill=red!20}]{U}\meter[style={fill=red!20}]{}\setwiretype{c}\\
\setwiretype{b}\gate[style={fill=red!20}]{P}\gate[style={fill=red!20}]{\text{wait}}\slice{\times T}

(547)

Note that here we have ancilla
|\text{anc}\rangle
preparation locations, 2-qubit and 1-qubit gate locations, wait locations, and measurement locations where faults may occur with rate
p
.
In the simplified model, we can abstract the locations inside the circuit to a “black-box” QEC round circuit with input errors happening before the entire
T
-round QEC cycle with rate
\tilde{p}
and for each of the
T
QEC rounds, syndrome bit-flip errors with rate
q
and data qubit errors with rate
p_{D}
:

\quantikz[rowsep=0.5cm,columnsep=0.5cm,classicalgap=0.05cm]\setwiretype{n}&\gate[2]{\text{QEC round}}\gate[1,style={fill=red!20}]{q}\setwiretype{c}\setwiretype{n}\\
\setwiretype{b}\gate[style={fill=red!20}]{\tilde{p}}\slice{}\gate[style={fill=red!20}]{p_{D}}\slice{\times T}\,.

(548)

We summarize the two models in the following table:

Aspect

Basic model

Simplified model

Scope

Full FT protocol: gates, EC, ancillas

Abstract QEC cycle (
T
SE rounds)

Noise

k
locations local stoch.
\leq p^{k}

\tilde{p},p,q

Location-based (gate/prep/meas/wait)

With these FT models and using the ingredients for the FTQC scheme we listed above, we can show that FTQC with constant space overhead can be achieved whenever error rates are below some thresholds.
In particular, this FTQC scheme uses a family of qLDPC codes
\{Q_{i}\}_{i}
with parameters
\llbracket n_{i},k_{i},d_{i}\rrbracket
satisfying: (1) a non-zero asymptotic rate
R=\lim_{n_{i}\rightarrow\infty}\frac{k_{i}}{n_{i}}
, (2) a condition on the growth of number of physical qubits
n_{i}
, and (3) existence of a decoding with logical error rate and residual error rate guarantees.
Using this qLDPC code family, we can show that a
k
-qubit logical circuit
C
with
f(k)
locations can be simulated by a circuit
\tilde{C}
using
O(k)
qubits at any given time and
O(f(k){\textrm{poly}\,}(k))
total number of physical locations, where the output distribution of
\tilde{C}
is
\epsilon
-far from
C
.
This is formalized in the following threshold theorem.

{thmbox}

[label=thm:constant_overhead_ftqc_threshold]Constant-overhead FTQC threshold
[
113
, Theorem 1]

Let
\{Q_{i}\}
be a family of QEC codes with:

1.

Q_{i}
is an
\llbracket n_{i},k_{i}\rrbracket

(r,c)
-LDPC code, for constants
r,c
.

2.

As
n_{i}\to\infty
,
\frac{k_{i}}{n_{i}}\to R>0
.

3.

0<n_{i}-n_{i-1}<n_{i-1}^{\beta}
for some
\beta>0
.

4.

Decoding guarantees local-stochastic noise:
Under local stochastic noise (with initialization error rate
\tilde{p}
per qubit, error rate in QEC cycle
p_{D}
per data qubit per syndrome extraction (SE), syndrome bit flip rate
q
),
\tilde{p}<p_{0}
,
p_{D}<p_{1}
, and
q<p_{2}
implies logical error
O(1/g(n_{i}))
after decoding and residual errors
\leq p_{0}/3
given a polynomial
T(n_{i})
syndrome extractions each with depth
h(n_{i})
if there is no logical errors.
(
T,h,g
are non-decreasing functions.)

Choose
\alpha<1
such that
0<\alpha\beta<1
.
Then, for all
\eta>1
,
\epsilon>0
and for all polynomials
f(n)=o(g(n^{\alpha}))
, there exists
p_{T}(\eta)
and
k_{0}(\eta,f,\epsilon)
such that for all sequential circuit
C
with
k>k_{0}
qubits and
f(k)
locations, there exists a simulation
\tilde{C}
using at most
\eta k/R
physical qubits.
If local-stochastic error rate
p
satisfies
p<p_{T}(\eta)
, statistical distance between
\tilde{C}
and
C
is at most
\epsilon>0
.
Furthermore for
\alpha^{\prime}=\max(\alpha,\alpha\beta)
, simulation
\tilde{C}
uses:

1.

O\big(\frac{f(k)T(2k^{\alpha^{\prime}})k^{\alpha^{\prime}}}{\eta-1}+f(k)k^{\alpha^{\prime}}\mathrm{polylog}(k/\epsilon)\big)
physical locations.

2.

Classical computation time of
O(h(2k^{\alpha^{\prime}})+\log\log(k/\epsilon))
per logical step.

3.

If
T(n_{i})
polynomial, then
|\tilde{C}|={\textrm{poly}\,}k
; if decoding can be done in polynomial time, then classical computation time complexity is also polynomial.

Note that the parameters
\beta>0
and
\alpha<1
determine the number of locations
{\texttt{loc}}(\tilde{C})
and the number of classical computation steps.
We will later see how these parameters are chosen.
Also, note that this threshold theorem holds for big enough logical circuits
C
, that is, ones that uses
k>k_{0}
qubits, where
k_{0}
also depends on these parameters.

14.4.2
Error correction

We now discuss how error correction is performed in this FTQC protocol, the rate at which errors remain, and how much overhead it incurs.
To perform reliable error correction, we measure each syndrome
T(n_{i})={\textrm{poly}\,}(n_{i})
times, where each syndrome measurement is done using Shor’s fault-tolerant error correction (Shor EC) scheme (c.f.
Section

13.2.1
).
For each stabilizer generator
g
with weight
w\leq r
, Shor EC for measuring
g
consists of three steps:

1.

Prepare an ancilla cat state
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|0^{w}\rangle+|1^{w}\rangle)
fault-tolerantly (will be discussed below).

2.

Apply controlled-Pauli gates from cat qubits to data qubits.

3.

Measure each ancilla qubit in
X
-basis.

For example, the Shor EC circuit to measure the syndrome of
X_{1}Z_{2}
is given by

\quantikz[rowsep=0.5cm,columnsep=0.5cm]\lstick[2]{|\text{cat}\rangle=\frac{|00\rangle+|11\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}}&\ctrl{2}\gate{H}\meter{}\rstick[2]{computeparity}\setwiretype{c}\\
\ctrl{2}\gate{H}\meter{}\setwiretype{c}\\
\lstick[2]{\text{data qubits}}\qw\gate{X}\qw\qw\\
\gate{Z}\qw\qw\qw

(549)

The cat state
\frac{|0^{r}\rangle+|1^{r}\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}
over
r
qubits can be prepared with low fault-probability using a gadget
\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{cat}}^{r}
that prepares the state and checks for bit-flip errors using pairwise
Z
measurement and
r^{\prime}
ancillas.
We then discard the output if the error check outputs a
-1
outcome and accept it otherwise.
For example, a gadget
\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{cat}}^{4}
that prepares
4
-qubit cat code using
r^{\prime}=1
check ancilla is given by

\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{cat}}^{4}=\quantikz\lstick[1]{|0\rangle}&\targ{}\ctrl{4}\rstick[4]{\frac{|0000\rangle+|1111\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}}\\
\lstick[1]{|0\rangle}\gate[1]{{{H}}}\ctrl{1}\ctrl{-1}\\
\lstick[1]{|0\rangle}\targ{}\ctrl{1}\\
\lstick[1]{|0\rangle}\targ{}\ctrl{1}\\
\setwiretype{n}\lstick[1]{|0\rangle}\targ{}\setwiretype{q}\targ{}\meter{Z}

(550)

where the two-qubit
Z
measurement checks the parity of the cat state.

Since each stabilizer generator has weight of at most
r
, a Shor EC needs an additional
r^{\prime}=O(r)
ancilla qubits per stabilizer generator (since we also need ancillas to check for errors in the cat state preparation).
Since we have
n_{i}-k_{i}
stabilizers to measure for each of the
M=\lceil k/k_{i}\rceil
code-blocks, a single round of Shor EC will need
r^{\prime}M(n_{i}-k_{i})
ancilla qubits if we measure all stabilizers in all code-blocks simultaneously.
To prevent this blowup, we split the
M
blocks of
\llbracket n_{i},k_{i},d_{i}\rrbracket
code to
s
sets, each containing
M/s
blocks.
Then, we measure only the syndromes of
M/s
code-blocks at any given time in the QEC cycle while all the other
(s-1)M/s
blocks wait until we measure all syndromes of the
M/s
code-blocks before we move on to the next
M/s
blocks.
This way, we only need additional
r^{\prime}M(n_{i}-k_{i})/s
ancilla qubits for QEC that we reuse to do Shor EC on different blocks in cycle.
Since we need to prepare an average of
\frac{1}{1-Ap}
cat states (as we dispose those that fail the error check), the total number of ancilla qubits we need for QEC is

\frac{r^{\prime}M(n_{i}-k_{i})}{s(1-Ap)}\,.

(551)

Now let us translate the error rate
p
in the basic model of fault tolerance to the physical data qubit error rate
p_{P}
and syndrome bit-flip error rate
p_{B}
to obtain the local-stochastic data qubit error rate
p_{D}
and syndrome bit-flip error rate
q
the simplified model for a QEC cycle.
Let us consider all fault locations in the SE circuit causing a physical data qubit error:

•

Cat state faults: cat state preparation error can propagate via controlled gates.
Each ancilla has
A
fault locations (dependent on
r
) and each qubit involved in at most
c
syndrome measurements.
So, the probability of qubit error from bad ancilla up to post-selection (with success probability
\geq 1-pA
) is
\frac{cAp}{1-pA}

•

Gate faults: at most
c
controlled-Pauli gates from each syndrome measurements the qubit is involved in, each with probability
p
.

•

Wait faults: idling errors during waits. Single syndrome measurement takes
l
time steps and measured every
s
cycles.
So each qubit has to wait at most for
sl
steps, each contributing to error probability
p
.

Thus, by putting all three error sources together, the physical data error rate
p_{D}
is given by:

p_{P}=\underbrace{\frac{cAp}{1-pA}}_{\text{ancilla propagation after post-selection}}+\underbrace{cp}_{\text{controlled gate error}}+\underbrace{slp}_{\text{wait time error}}

(552)

Note that the data qubit error rate satisfy local stochastic condition:
\Pr[a\text{ data errors}]\leq p_{P}^{a}
because Shor SE is fault-tolerant (see
Section

13.3.1
).
Now let us consider all fault locations in the SE circuit causing a syndrome bit-flip error:

•

Cat state faults: similar to the physical data qubit faults above, faults in the cat state preparation circuit causes bit-flip error with probability
\frac{Ap}{1-pA}
.

•

Gate and measurement faults: there are
r
controlled-Pauli,
r
Hadamard gates, and
r
measurements in an SE circuit, where each location fails with probability
p
.
Thus the probability of a bit-flip error from gate and measurement faults is
3rp
.

Putting the two error sources together gives a syndrome bit-flip error rate of

p_{B}=\underbrace{\frac{Ap}{1-pA}}_{\text{Cat-state prep}}+\underbrace{rp}_{\text{controlled-Paulis}}+\underbrace{rp}_{\text{Hadamard gates}}+\underbrace{rp}_{\text{measurements}}\,.

(553)

Note that there are correlations between data qubit errors and syndrome errors, where a physical data error in the basic FT model can cause both syndrome bit-flip errors and data qubit errors in the simplified model.
For example, suppose that a qubit
j
is involved in stabilizers
g_{1},\dots,g_{5}
, measured in this sequence.
Then, suppose that a physical error
E
at qubit
j
after measurement
g_{3}
but before
g_{4}
in the first round of SE, and that this error anticommutes with all five stabilizers.
Then, this error will flip syndromes
g_{4},g_{5}
in the first SE round and then flip
g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}
in the second SE round while
g_{4},g_{5}
remains the same (assuming there have been no other errors), as illustrated in the following:

\quantikz[rowsep=0.5cm,columnsep=0.5cm,classicalgap=0.05cm]\setwiretype{n}&\gate[2]{\text{SE round 1}}\setwiretype{c}\setwiretype{n}\gate[2]{\text{SE round 2}}\setwiretype{c}\\

but only
g_{1}
and

Thus, we translate this fault

in the basic FT model to a data qubit error

and syndrome bit errors on

in the first round of SE.

On the other hand, if error
E
at qubit
j
happens after measurement
g_{1}
but before
g_{2}
in the second round of SE, it will flip
g_{2},\dots,g_{5}
:
